## A researcher's freedom to decide

As researchers we make lots of decisions throughout the life cycle of a
research project: Which hypotheses to test? How big a sample size is
needed? How long should the data collection period be? Which statistical
test(s) is most appropriate? Because of the great flexibility in how
research can be conducted (known as researcher degrees of freedom),
**how** and **when** we make these decisions matters for the credibility
of science.

Generally researchers accept a 5% false-positive rate (*p* ≤ .05) when
testing a hypothesis. In other words, 20 attempts to investigate a false
hypothesis will result in one statistical result [@simmons2021]. In
practical terms, the more statistical tests we do the more likely we are
to falsely find a statistically significant result (see example below).

::: {.callout-note title="How false positive results can happen"}
Say you are trying to test whether female bird species X prefer males
with larger feathers. You are unsure of the effect size or how big a
sample size to collect, so you begin with collecting data on 10 females.
With the sample size of 10 you run a simple regression to test whether
feather length predicts female response Y. The regression reveals a
trend showing females have a slight preference for larger feathers, but
this result is not statistically significant. You are drawn to the
result and think that a significant result can be reached by increasing
the statistical power. You decide to collect more data on 10 more
females, as a way to improve the statistical power, and rerun your
regression with the 20 females.

In pursuit of the significant result, you have inadvertently increased
your false positive rate from 5% to \~7.7% (based on @simmons2011 false
positive simulation study). This occurred because the two datasets were
combined in the analysis and therefore are not independent resulting in
an increased chance of reaching a significant result. The risk of
reaching a false positive finding increases the more times you cycle
through data collection and significance testing then collecting more
data and so on. This is why a data collection stopping rule decided in
advance during the study design stage! More on this in [how to
preregister section](preregistration-components.qmd).

This example has been adapted from @forstmeier2017.

:::

In addition to post-hoc decisions like in the example described above,
researchers can follow an exploratory, hypothesis-generating approach
and then report their outcomes as grounded in theory and planned. Other
times researchers can decide to report the "best" studies from a series
of studies and label the other studies as "failures". Even to refining
the study design while exploring the data. As researchers we are keen to
make sure our approaches are "right", yet we do not always account for
our biases or forget what we originally planned. The issues raised by
this flexible decision making process comes under the umbrella of
questionable research practices (QRPs). We will cover the topic of QRPs
in more detail in the [Questionable research practices](qrps.qmd) page.

::: callout-important
Recognizing the difference between exploratory and hypothesis testing
approaches both as a *contributor* to and *consumer* of research is
critical for transparent and credible science [@nosek2018].
:::

## Questioning how we do research

A core role of a scientist is to discover truths about how the world
works. We can generate hypotheses, collect data, then examine the data
and interpret findings in relation to our hypotheses to hopefully build
more theories about how the world works. Research is built on prior
findings. The publication of false positive findings due to questionable
research practices has implications within and beyond academic research.
It can lead to incorrect conclusions potentially resulting in wasted
resources for researchers inspired to build upon the (incorrect)
findings. This can also result in ineffective policy recommendations or
even harmful medical interventions [@simmons2021].

::: {.callout-note title="Reflection point" collapse="true"}
When decisions are made in the research process are often not clearly
communicated in a typical published study.

Think about the last published study you read, can you tell if the
research questions or hypotheses were formulated *before* or *after* the
study findings were known, and does this matter?

Short answer is: no, you cannot really tell and yes it does matter!
:::

Over the past couple of decades, researchers primarily in the field of
psychology raised major concerns about the credibility of science
("credibility/reproducibility/replicability crisis") as many studies
were unable to be replicated [@opensciencecollaboration2015]. Engaging
in questionable research practices have been cited as key contributors
to this "crisis".

::: {.callout-note title="Structural contributions to the crisis" collapse="false"}
Other cited contributors to the "crisis" were structural issues relating
to academic incentive structure, publish or perish culture,
prioritization of research novelty over replication. It is important to
be aware of these factors, but note addressing them is beyond the sphere
of influence of the majority of researchers. We will focus this tutorial
on what concrete actions we as researchers and teams can do improve how
we do science.
:::

![Figure adapted from @ihle2024;
@centerforopenscience2026.](images/credibility-crisis.png){fig-alt="A screenshot of journal articles highlighting the credibility crisis over the last two decades."
fig-align="center" width="602"}

Recognizing the challenges in how science is conducted, researchers have
calls for a more optimistic framing of the crisis to one of a
"credibility revolution" [@vazire2018a; @fanelli2018a]. This reframing
outlines where we as individual researchers have agency to adopt more
transparent and reproducible ways of working in order to ensure
scientific progress.

## Preregistration as part of the credibility revolution

A strategy to address the "crisis" is the practice of study
preregistration. Preregistrations aim to:

- reduce questionable research practices and bias

- increase transparency

- clarify exploratory vs hypothesis testing.

This is works by producing an uneditable time-stamped document that
outlines a study plan including research questions/hypotheses, research
design, data analysis *before* data collection and analysis. A study
preregistration is then uploaded onto a verified repository so that it
can be publicly shared with others (possibly after an embargo period)
[@nosek2018; @parsons2022]. Importantly, preregistration does not favor
hypothesis testing approach over exploratory methods to research, but
instead aims to clearly differentiate between the two.

::: callout-caution
### Terminology

You may notice in the literature different terms relating to
preregistration like *study registration*. Some researchers are
advocating for a reform of terms to avoid ambiguity, as some terms can
refer to different practices occurring at various stages of the research
life cycle [@mayo-wilson2025]. In this tutorial, we will use the term
preregistration.
:::

One of the earliest formal implementations of registrations comes from
medical clinical trials. More recently, researchers and journals in the
field of psychology have rapidly adopted this practice. Preregistration
is relevant to all kinds of research:

- **Qualitative** (interview study, focus groups, ethnographic)
- **Review-based** (systematic, narrative)
- **Intervention/experimental** (randomized control trials, factorial
  design)
- **Observational** (case study, natural experiment, longitudinal)

::: callout-note
### Did you know?

The concept of preregistration is not new! The scientist and philosopher
Charles Sanders Peirce in \~1880s created a set of rules to test "the
truth", with one being that hypotheses should be stated *before* data
collection [@peirce1883].
:::

Being able to understand the different research approaches, study
designs and key concepts will help provide context for the steps
required to do a study preregistration. We will explore some [research
methods](research-cycle.qmd) later on.

### What would you do?

Imagine if your PhD lab mate Max came to you with this dilemma:

"I've been analyzing the data from my first thesis chapter (which I
really want to publish, as it will help with my chances of getting a
post doc). One of my hypotheses is that X influences Y. I've measured
many variables to test this hypothesis. However during the data
analysis, results seem to show X has no effect on Y, unless I remove a
variable. Do you have any suggestions of what I should do?"

What would you recommend Max does from the options listed below?

- [ ] A) Remove that variable from the analysis

- [ ] B) Tweak the hypothesis to match the results

- [ ] C) Collect more data in the hope, a larger sample size will show
  an effect

- [ ] D) Try out a new statistical test to see if there is a significant
  effect

- [ ] E) Leave that variable in and write up the results as they are

::: {.callout-note title="Reveal answer" collapse="true"}
Option E would be the recommended approach at this stage. This option
acknowledges the current challenges Max is facing analyzing their data,
without further compromising the integrity of their research. Max can
use this first thesis chapter as a learning experience and improve their
research practices in their next project.
:::

We will revisit Max's dilemma throughout this tutorial and hopefully by
the end you will be more confident at identifying potential issues and
recognize how preregistration can help safeguard against questionable
research practice and promote more credible research.

## Summary

- Researchers make a lot of decisions during the research process

- **How** and **when** researchers make these decisions matters for the
  credibility of science

- Preregistration is a practice that aims to reduce bias, increase
  transparency, clarify exploratory vs hypothesis testing.
